name: Chandas
description: Pingala's poetic meters as the corners of a cube in 3 to 7 dimensions, turning through hidden dimensions.
aria: A cube of light in higher dimensions whose corners are Pingala's meters
intro: Every poetic meter Pingala counted is a corner of a cube in higher dimensions. Here is that cube, turning through the fourth dimension.
legend: corner = one meter, labelled । light ऽ heavy
gold spark: walks through every meter

tutorial.t: A meter is a pattern of light and heavy
tutorial.b: Sanskrit verse is built from syllables that are either laghu, light (।), or guru, heavy (ऽ). Over 2,000 years ago Pingala listed every possible pattern. With 3 syllables there are 8: ।।।, ।।ऽ, ।ऽ।, and so on.
tutorial.see: the 8 labels on the cube's corners. That's every 3-syllable meter, once each.

tutorial.b: Write ऽ as 0 and । as 1, read the digits right to left, and a meter becomes a binary number. Pingala's rules for listing all the meters (prastāra) and for finding a meter's place in that list (uddiṣṭa) then work exactly like counting in binary. Give each syllable its own direction in space and each meter becomes a corner: 3 syllables, 3 directions, a cube.
tutorial.see: the first symbol of each label changes when you cross the cube one way, the second when you cross it another.

tutorial.b: Two corners are joined only if their meters differ in exactly one syllable. The edge's colour says which syllable. Gold edges flip the first syllable, orange the second, rose the third. The key at the bottom left lists them.
tutorial.see: pick a gold edge and compare the labels at its two ends. Only the first symbol differs.

tutorial.b: The gold spark visits every meter exactly once, changing one syllable per step (a Gray code). The big symbols at the bottom show the meter it's on, and the syllable that just changed glows. Each step plays a note: more heavy syllables means a higher note.
tutorial.see: the bottom caption, and listen: the pitch climbs as heavy syllables appear.

tutorial.t: One more syllable, one more dimension
tutorial.b: With 4 syllables there are 16 meters, and you need a 4th direction: a tesseract. A screen can only show 3, so it's drawn the way a photo shows a 3D box, with the far side smaller. That's why you see a cube inside a cube.
tutorial.see: the violet edges joining the inner cube to the outer one. They flip syllable 4: the inner cube is every meter ending in one way, the outer cube the other.

tutorial.b: In 4D you don't rotate around an axis, you rotate in a plane, two directions at once. This turns the plane of syllables 1 and 4: the inner and outer cubes swap places. The faint panes show the squares lying in that plane. Drag the scene to turn the ordinary 3 directions yourself.
tutorial.see: the inner cube grow outward while the outer one shrinks in. No edge ever breaks.

tutorial.b: How many squares, cubes, edges? A k-dimensional face frees k syllables and fixes the rest: C(n,k)·2ⁿ⁻ᵏ. The C(n,k) come from the meru-prastāra, the stepped 'mountain' Halāyudha read out of Pingala's rules, centuries before Pascal. The tesseract has 16 corners, 32 edges, 24 squares and 8 cubes.
tutorial.see: now 5 syllables, 32 meters. Ask the guide 'show me 7 dimensions', or press n for the full working.

sound:
The spark sings the meter. At each step a santoor note plays, pitched by how many heavy syllables the meter has: ।।।। sits at the bottom, every extra ऽ is one step up the scale, ऽऽऽऽ at the top. Because the walk changes one syllable at a time, the melody only ever moves one step up or down. You're hearing the Gray code.

A singing bowl rings each time a new plane starts turning.

Every chamber plays in Raag Bhupali: five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as whole-number ratios of the home note Sa (138.6 Hz here): 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up every few cycles, so they never clash. That lets the math pick any note it likes and it still sounds like music. Underneath, a tanpura drone holds Sa and Pa, and a bansuri improvises in the same raag. The santoor and the singing bowl are the ones the math plays.

faq.a: Laghu (।) is a light, short syllable; guru (ऽ) is heavy, either a long vowel or a short one followed by two consonants. Sanskrit meters are patterns of the two.

Any two-symbol code works: with 2 choices per syllable there are 2ⁿ meters of n syllables. Pingala's prastāra lists them in an order that matches binary counting if guru = 0, laghu = 1 and the digits are read right to left; his uddiṣṭa rule recovers a meter's position the same way.
Each syllable is one direction. 4 syllables need 4 directions, so the meters sit on the corners of a 4D cube. The screen shows a perspective shadow of it, the way a drawing shows a 3D box.

faq.q: why is there a cube inside a cube?
faq.a: That's perspective in the 4th direction: the half of the tesseract that's further away in 4D is drawn smaller. Inner cube: syllable 4 one way. Outer cube: the other.

faq.q: what is the gold spark doing?
faq.a: Walking a reflected Gray code: every meter once, one syllable changed per step, g(i) = i XOR (i >> 1). It's a Hamiltonian cycle on the hypercube.

faq.q: what do the edge colours mean?
faq.a: An edge joins two meters that differ in one syllable, and its colour says which: gold 1st, orange 2nd, rose 3rd, violet 4th, blue 5th, green 6th, cream 7th.

A stepped triangle of numbers, the binomial coefficients, that Halāyudha read out of Pingala's sutras in the 10th century. It counts meters with k heavy syllables, and also the faces of the n-cube: C(n,k)·2ⁿ⁻ᵏ.
The author of the Chandaḥśāstra, a treatise on Sanskrit prosody from around the 3rd to 2nd century BCE. Halāyudha's 10th-century commentary spells out the combinatorics.
Bhupali uses five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as the ratios 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2 and 5/3. It has no half-steps, so any note the math picks sounds consonant against the drone.

Sa is 138.6 Hz. Every other note is Sa times a whole-number ratio (9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3) or that times a power of 2 for higher octaves. Which note plays is chosen by a number in the scene. Open 'why this sound' to watch it live.
The haze behind the math is a kaleidoscope shader. Its symmetry follows the chamber's math, but it's decoration. Say 'trip 0' to switch it off and see only the math.
Isha Maini, a data science student at Emory. Each chamber's math is written and tested in Python and JavaScript before it's drawn.
